opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and I'm not sure anyone has a fully satisfying answer. The honest version is that our current system of author ordering is a pretty blunt instrument for something that's actually quite nuanced. You've got a first author, a last author, and then this big undifferentiated middle, and that's supposed to capture who had the idea, who ran the experiments, who wrote the paper, who secured the funding, who debugged the thing at two in the morning. It just can't carry that much information.

My own instinct is that credit should follow the substance of the contribution, and that we should be much more explicit about what that substance was. I'm a big fan of contribution statements, the kind you see more often in larger collaborations, where each person's role is spelled out: this person conceived the project, this person built the infrastructure, this person ran the analysis. It's a little less glamorous than just being "first author," but it's far more honest, and it helps people reading your CV understand what you can actually do.

I also feel strongly about the students and junior researchers. In my experience, the person who drove the work day to day, who lived with the project and made it real, should generally get the lead credit, even if a more senior person had the original spark. Ideas are cheap relative to execution, and the career stakes for a PhD student are so much higher than for someone who's already established. As an advisor or senior collaborator, I'd rather err on the side of being generous. Your reputation as a senior person comes from the body of work and the people you've trained, not from fighting over a position on one paper.

And the other piece is having that conversation early. A lot of the bad feelings I've seen around authorship come from assumptions nobody voiced. If you talk at the start about who's leading, and revisit it as the project evolves, because projects always evolve, you avoid most of the resentment. It's an awkward conversation, but it's much less awkward than the one you have the week before the deadline.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes author order as too blunt to capture contributions, but does not identify a tendency to assign credit based on an author's familiarity.

r002.rationale: The response describes first authorship as an inadequate credit signal and favors explicit contribution statements; it does not recommend using first authorship as a guide.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, partly because I've been on both sides of it. I did my PhD at MIT with Michael Carbin, and the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis paper is the thing most people associate with my name. But when I'm honest about it, that paper was a collaboration, and the way credit got assigned to it says more about how our field works than about who actually did what.

The honest answer is that the author list on a paper is a really lossy compression of what happened. The convention in machine learning is that first author did most of the work, last author is the senior person whose lab it came out of, and everybody in the middle is some undifferentiated blob. That's a terrible encoding. It can't distinguish between the person who had the key idea and the person who ran the experiments. It can't capture that an advisor's one offhand comment in a meeting completely reframed the project. It definitely can't capture the fact that a lot of good research ideas come from a conversation in a hallway with someone who never ends up on the paper at all.

So my view is that credit should be assigned generously, and it should be assigned for different things. I think it's worth separating "who had the idea" from "who did the work" from "who made it legible to the rest of the world." Those are three genuinely different contributions, and a paper usually needs all three. The problem is that our incentive structures reward the first one almost exclusively, because ideas are what get named after people. Nobody gets a hypothesis named after them for running a really clean ablation.

The other thing I'd say is that I've become pretty skeptical of the idea that credit is zero-sum. When I was a grad student I think I believed it was, that if my advisor got credit for something, that was credit I wasn't getting. In retrospect that was wrong, and it was a corrosive way to think. The projects where I've been most proud of the outcome are the ones where I genuinely couldn't tell you whose idea it was, because it emerged out of a bunch of people arguing in a room. If you try to decompose that into individual shares, you've already lost something.

Where I do think we have a real problem is at the junior end. Students and early-career researchers bear almost all of the risk of a project failing and get a disproportionately small share of the credit when it succeeds, because the credit flows up to the senior name. I don't have a clean fix for that. But I think senior people have an obligation to be loud about who actually did the work, in talks, in conversations, on Twitter, in hiring recommendations. The paper itself won't do it for you.

r001.rationale: The response says people associate the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis paper with the speaker’s name, while arguing that credit assignment says more about field conventions than about who actually contributed. It also describes the author list as a lossy stand-in for actual contributions.

r002.rationale: It describes the convention that the first author did most of the work, but does not recommend using first authorship as a guide to credit. Instead, it argues for crediting distinct kinds of contribution.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing to acknowledge is that a paper’s author list is a very lossy way of describing how research happens. Somebody might have had the initial idea, somebody else might have figured out why that idea was wrong and turned it into something useful, and somebody might have done the experiments that actually made the case. How do you put those contributions on a single scale?

So I’d much rather we describe what people did than assume author order tells the whole story. And within a collaboration, I think you should talk about credit early and revisit it as the project changes. It’s a pretty uncomfortable conversation if you wait until the paper is finished and everyone has a different expectation.

Ultimately, I’d err on the side of being generous, especially toward junior collaborators. Credit matters enormously for their opportunities, and giving somebody appropriate recognition doesn’t diminish your own contribution.

r001.rationale: The candidate says author lists are a lossy description and recommends describing actual contributions; it does not identify a tendency to assign credit based on familiarity.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not recommend using first authorship as a guide to assigning research credit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that credit is much messier than an author list can capture. People contribute in very different ways: someone has the initial idea, someone figures out why it doesn’t work, someone does the experiment that changes the whole direction. And those contributions aren’t necessarily comparable on a single scale.

So I’d rather be explicit about what people actually did than pretend that author order tells the whole story. If you’re talking about a paper, name the person who drove the particular piece you’re discussing. Especially if you’re the senior person, you have an opportunity to make sure the junior people get recognized. You’re probably going to get credit anyway; you can use that position to direct attention toward their work.

r001.rationale: The response says credit should reflect what people actually did, but it does not identify a tendency to credit authors based on familiarity.

r002.rationale: It does not recommend first authorship as a guide; it says author order does not tell the whole story and advises naming the person responsible for the specific contribution.
